FIFA WORLD CUP DATA INTELLIGENCE

Project documentation

A practical guide to the project’s source datasets, SQL database, Python notebooks, validation checks, analytics, and local run steps.

Project at a glance

The project combines historical World Cup records with 2026 match analytics in a relational database and a web analytics experience.

17Tables
37Relationships
211,808Records
1,352Matches
31Tournaments

Data sources

  • Historical World Cup tournaments, teams, players, matches, goals, bookings, substitutions, stadiums, and attendance.
  • 2026 match and player performance data, including passing networks.
  • FIFA ranking snapshots and ranking points.
  • Official 2026 stadium location and capacity data.
  • 2026 player team, position, and birth-date information.

Download the CSV source package from Fifa worldcup data.zip.

SQL workflow

  1. 01_create_database.sql — Create the database schema, tables, keys, and constraints.
  2. 02_bulk_insert_all.sql — Load source CSV files in relationship order.
  3. 03_update_missing_data.sql — Apply supported data corrections and complete missing details.
  4. 04_analytical_queries.sql — Run 32 analytical queries and create the reusable team performance view.

The downloadable SQL archive contains all four scripts.

Data analysis

01_data_analysis.ipynb

04_sql_to_python_analysis.ipynb

Validation results

The saved validation report covers 13 cleaned CSV tables and 69,309 records. Primary-key, foreign-key, match, score, date, and duplicate checks pass.

Attendance / capacity: WARN. 99 records exceed the linked stadium capacity and are flagged for review. The report does not claim every check passed.

Database and ERD

The relational model contains 17 tables and 37 relationships. Open erd/FIFA_WorldCup_ERD.html to explore the interactive database diagram.

Available analytics

  • Historical men's World Cup goals per match, 1930–2026.
  • Expected goals compared with actual goals in 2026 matches.
  • FIFA pre-tournament rankings compared with 2026 team win rates.
  • Player appearances and goals across tournaments.

Run the project

  1. Download the source data, SQL archive, and Python notebooks.
  2. Set up SQL Server and create the project database.
  3. Run the four SQL scripts in order, configuring source paths for your environment.
  4. Open the notebooks in Jupyter; configure CSV paths and the SQL Server connection where needed.
  5. From the web app folder, run npm install, then npm run dev.

The Python notebooks do not include a shared requirements file; install the packages imported by the notebook you plan to run.
